en: The Questions in the Verses of the Pārāyana Chapter from the Cūḷaniddesa
1. The Question of the Young Brahmin Ajita “By what, indeed, is the world enveloped?
(Thus spoke the Venerable Ajita.)
Why does it not shine forth?
What do you say is its defilement?
And what is its greatest fear?”
“The world is shrouded by ignorance,
Ajita,” said the Blessed One,
“and through stinginess and negligence it does not shine forth.”
I call craving the defilement;
suffering is its great terror.
Streams flow everywhere—
(Thus spoke the Venerable Ajita:
"What is the obstruction of the streams?
Tell me the restraint of the streams."
“By what are the streams blocked?
“The streams that exist in the world,” [said the Blessed One,] “Ajita, ... [are blocked by wisdom].”
Mindfulness is their prevention;
I call it the restraint of the streams.
By means of wisdom, these are closed off.
“Wisdom and mindfulness as well,
O venerable Ajita,
and name-and-form, my dear sir;”
"Being asked this, tell me:
where does this come to an end?
"Regarding this question you have asked..."
I tell you this, Ajita:
that place where both name-and-form cease without remainder.
With the cessation of consciousness,
this is here brought to an end.
And those who have realized the Dhamma...
"And those many who here are still in training—
being asked, O Wise One, tell me their mode of conduct, dear sir."
“One should not covet sensual pleasures,
nor be turbid in mind;
one should be skilled in all phenomena.”
“A mindful bhikkhu should wander forth.
Thus ends the first inquiry of the young brahmin Ajita. 2.
The Inquiry of the Young Brahmin Tissa Metteyya.
“Contented in the world regarding anger,” said the Venerable Tissa Metteyya,
“for whom are there no more disturbances?”
Who, having directly known both ends,
does not cling to the middle through wisdom?
Whom do you call a "Great Man"?
“Who here has transcended the seamstress?
“One who lives the holy life regarding sensual pleasures,” [said the Blessed One, “Metteyya”].
Free from craving, always mindful,
the bhikkhu who has attained Nibbāna through full understanding—
of him there are no more fluctuations.
Thus, having directly known both ends,
the wise one is not defiled by the middle;
him I call a Great Man.
Thus, here he has transcended the seamstress.
This was the second inquiry of the young brahmin Tissa Metteyya.
3. The Inquiry of the Young Brahmin Puṇṇaka.
“O you who see the root of the unshaken,
I have come with a question,” said the Venerable Puṇṇaka.
Upon what did the seers, men,
kshatriyas, brahmins, and deities rely when they performed various sacrifices here in the world?
“I ask you, Blessed One, please tell me this.
“Whosoever these sages among men may be,
Puṇṇaka,” said the Blessed One.
Khattiyas and brahmins,
O Puṇṇaka, desiring this very state of existence, have here in the world performed many sacrifices for the sake of the deities.
“Those who have been worn down by old age performed sacrifices.
“Whosoever these seers among men may be,” said the Venerable Puṇṇaka.
Khattiyas and brahmins have performed many sacrifices here in the world for the sake of the deities;
O Blessed One, did they remain diligent on the path of sacrifice?
They have crossed over birth and old age, dear sir;
I ask you, Blessed One, tell me this.
“They pray, they praise, they invoke, and they offer oblations.”
"O Puṇṇaka," said the Blessed One,
"they long for sensual pleasures depending on gain;
devoted to sacrifice, they are stained by passion for existence."
“I say they have not transcended birth and old age.
“If those engaged in sacrifice have not transcended them,” said the Venerable Puṇṇaka.
By means of sacrifices, O dear sir, one may transcend both birth and old age;
but who indeed in the world of gods and men has truly crossed over birth and old age, O dear sir?
“I ask you, Blessed One, tell me this.
“Having discerned the high and low in the world, Puṇṇaka,” said the Blessed One, “... [the one who knows the world as it really is].”
He who has no agitation anywhere in the world—
peaceful, smokeless, free from distress, and desireless—
he has crossed over birth and old age; of him I say this.
The third inquiry: The Question of the Young Brahmin Puṇṇaka.
4. The Question of the Young Brahmin Mettagū:
“I ask you, Blessed One, please tell me this.”
(Thus spoke the Venerable Mettagū:
"I consider you to be one who has attained knowledge and developed the self;
from where, indeed, have these sufferings arisen?"
“Whatever various forms there are in the world.
“You are indeed asking me about the origin of suffering,” said the Blessed One to Mettagū.
I shall declare that to you according to my understanding:
whatever various kinds of suffering arise in the world, they all originate from the source of clinging.
The fool who, being ignorant, creates acquisitions,
repeatedly encounters suffering;
therefore, one who understands should not create acquisitions.
“Observing the origin of suffering through birth.
“That which we asked you, you have explained to us;
now we ask another thing—please tell us that.”
“How indeed do the wise cross over the flood,
birth, old age, sorrow, and lamentation?
O Sage, please explain this well to me.”
"For this Dhamma is known to you.
"I shall proclaim the Dhamma to you," [said the Blessed One,] Mettagū.
Having understood that which is not based on tradition in this very life,
one who dwells mindful shall cross over attachment to the world.
“And I rejoice in that supreme Dhamma, O Great Seer;
having understood it, one should live mindfully.”
“Cross over the attachment to the world.
“Whatever you perceive, Mettagū,” said the Blessed One, “... [cross over it].”
Above, below, across, and in the middle—
having dispelled both delight and settling in these,
consciousness shall not remain in existence.
Dwelling thus, mindful and vigilant,
the bhikkhu who moves about, having abandoned all things cherished as "mine," [transcends] birth,
old age, sorrow, and lamentation.
“Right here, the wise one should abandon suffering.
“I delight in these words of the Great Seer,
well-proclaimed by Gotama as being free from acquisitions.”
Truly, the Blessed One has abandoned suffering,
for this Dhamma is known by you.
Surely they too shall abandon suffering.
O Sage, you who would advise one who stands firm—
approaching you, O Naga, I pay homage to you,
so that perhaps the Blessed One might advise me as well while I stand firm.
“That brahmin whom one should know as a possessor of true knowledge—
one who possesses nothing and is unattached to sensual existence—
has surely crossed over this flood.”
Having crossed over, free from harshness and doubt,
the wise man who has attained knowledge here,
having relinquished this attachment to becoming and non-becoming;
"Thus, free from craving, untroubled, and without hope,
he has crossed over birth and old age— so I say.
This is the fourth inquiry of the youth Mettagū.
5. The Inquiry of the Young Brahmin Dhotaka “I ask you, Blessed One;
tell me this,” [said the Venerable Dhotaka].
O Great Seer, I long for your voice;
having heard your utterance,
I shall train myself for my own Nibbāna.
“Therefore, exert yourself with ardor,
O Dhota, (said the Blessed One),
being wise and mindful right here.”
Having heard this cry, one should train for one's own Nibbāna:
"In the world of gods and humans, I see..."
I pay homage to that Brahmin who wanders as one possessing nothing, O All-Seeing One;
release me from my doubts, O Sakka!
“I will not tolerate anyone in the world who wavers in their views, O Dhotaṅka;
for I have realized the supreme Dhamma.”
“Thus you have crossed over this flood.
“O Brahmā, out of compassion,
instruct me so that I may understand the Dhamma of seclusion.”
"Just as space is unafflicted, so may I,
being at peace right here, dwell without dependence.
"I shall proclaim your peace to you."
(The Blessed One said: "O Dhotaka,
that which is known in this very life, not based on tradition—
having understood this, one should live mindfully."
"Cross over the attachment to the world.
"And I rejoice in that,
O Great Seer, the supreme peace;"
“Having understood that, practicing with mindfulness,
one crosses over attachment to the world.
“Whatever you are fully aware of...”
(Dhotaka, said the Blessed One:
"Above, below, across, and in the middle—
having understood this as a snare in the world,"
"Do not create craving for existence and non-existence.
This was the fifth inquiry of the young man Dhota. 6.
The Inquiry of the Young Man Upasīva.
“Alone, O Sakka, I am unable to cross over the great flood without support,” said the Venerable Upasīva.
"Tell me the object, O All-Seeing One,
by relying upon which I might cross over this flood.
"Perceiving nothingness, mindful,"
"Upasīva," said the Blessed One,
"cross over the flood by relying on 'it does not exist';
having abandoned sensual pleasures, be detached from talk."
Behold the destruction of craving as the supreme night-watch!
He who is free from passion for all sensual pleasures—
thus spoke the Venerable Upasīva.
Relying on nothingness and having abandoned conceiving,
being supremely liberated through the deliverance of perception—
would he remain there, no longer following after [conditioned things]?
“He who is free from passion for all sensual desires,
Upasīva,” said the Blessed One,
“and relies on the state of nothingness, having abandoned the conceit ‘I am’;”
“Completely released and supreme in the liberation from perceptions,
he would abide there, no longer following after them.
“If he were to abide there, no longer following after them...”
Even for many years, O All-Seeing One,
he would remain right there, cooled and liberated;
yet for one such as that, consciousness would eventually pass away.
“Just as a flame cast by the force of the wind,
Upasīva,” said the Blessed One,
“goes out and cannot be reckoned.”
Thus the sage, liberated from the group of names,
passes away and does not enter into reckoning.
"Has he gone to destruction, or does he not exist?"
Or is one indeed healthy for all eternity?
O Sage, please explain this clearly to me,
for this Dhamma is known to you.
“There is no measure for one who has gone to cessation,” said the Blessed One, “Upasīva;
that by which they might describe him does not exist for him.”
“When all phenomena have been eradicated,
all paths of speech are also eradicated.
This is the sixth inquiry of the young man Upasīva.
7. The Inquiry of the Young Brahmin Nanda “There are sages in the world,” [said the venerable Nanda].
People speak thus: "How is this?
They say of us, "The Sage is endowed with knowledge," or perhaps, "He is endowed with life."
“Neither by view, nor by hearsay, nor by knowledge do the sages here,
O Nanda, declare one to be skilled;
having become free from enmity, free from distress, and free from desire— ”
“Those who wander, I call them sages.
“Whosoever these ascetics and brahmins may be,” said the Venerable Nanda.
They say purification comes through what is seen and heard;
they say purification comes through rules and observances;
they speak of purification in many various ways.
"Will those who practice with restraint there, O Blessed One, have crossed over birth and old age, O Venerable Sir?
I ask you this, Blessed One; please tell me this."
“Whatever recluses and brahmins there may be,
O Nanda,” said the Blessed One,
“they claim purification even through what is seen or heard;”
They say purification comes through rules and observances, they say purification comes through various forms [of practice];
though they may conduct themselves with restraint therein, [they are not purified].
“I say they have transcended birth and aging.
“Whosoever these ascetics and brahmins may be,” said the Venerable Nanda.
They say purification comes through what is seen or heard;
they say purification comes through rules and observances;
they speak of purification in many different ways.
If you say that those sages have not crossed over the flood,
then who indeed in the world of gods and humans,
O Blessed One, has crossed over birth and old age?
“I ask you, Blessed One, please tell me this.
“I do not say that all ascetics and brahmins [are happy],
Nanda,” said the Blessed One.
I say they are shrouded by birth and old age—
those who here have abandoned everything seen, heard, or sensed, as well as all rules and observances.
Having abandoned all manifold forms and having fully understood craving, those who are free from taints—
them indeed I call people who have crossed the flood.
“I rejoice in these words of the Great Seer,
so well-proclaimed by Gotama regarding the state beyond acquisitions:
those things here that have been seen, heard, or sensed— ”
Having abandoned all rules and observances,
having abandoned all various forms,
and having fully understood craving, they are free from taints.
“I too declare that I have crossed over the flood.
Thus ends the seventh inquiry, the Question of the Young Brahmin Nanda. 8.
The Question of the Young Brahmin Hemaka.
“Those who previously explained things to me,” (said the Venerable Hemaka),
“before the teaching of Gotama.”
"It was thus," "it will be thus"—
all that is mere hearsay;
all that is merely an increase of speculative reasoning.
I found no delight there.
O Sage, you who have destroyed craving, please teach me the Dhamma that brings about its destruction.
"Having understood this and practicing with mindfulness,
one crosses over attachment to the world.
"In this regard, regarding what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized..."
O Hemaka, the dispelling of desire and lust for pleasant forms is the deathless state of Nibbāna.
Having understood this, those who are mindful,
having attained final nibbāna in this very life,
are forever at peace.
“Having crossed over attachment to the world.
Thus ends the eighth inquiry, that of the young man Hemaka.
9. The Inquiry of the Young Man Todeyya.
“In whom sensual desires do not dwell,
(so said the Venerable Todeyya,) and in whom craving is no longer found;”
"And for one who has crossed over doubt,
what kind of liberation is his?
"In that wherein sensual desires do not dwell..."
"Toḍeyya," said the Blessed One,
"is one in whom craving no longer exists,
who has crossed over all doubt."
For him there is no further liberation.
Is he without hope, or is he still hoping?
Is he one possessed of wisdom, or is he merely fashioning wisdom?
“Sakka, tell me how I may recognize a sage,
O All-Seeing One. “He is one who has no longing and does not long for anything;”
He possesses wisdom and does not construct with wisdom;
know him thus, Todeyya, to be a sage,
possessing nothing and unattached to sensual existence.
The ninth is the Question of the Young Brahmin Todeyya. 10.
The Question of the Young Brahmin Kappa:
“Of those standing in the middle of the lake, ...”
(Thus spoke the Venerable Kappa:
When the flood has arisen with its great terrors,
for those who are overcome by old age and death,
Speak of an island, dear sir;
you yourself explain the island to me,
so that there may be no further becoming.
“Standing in the middle of a lake,
O Kappa,” said the Blessed One,
“when a great and terrifying flood has arisen;”
I declare you to be an island for those overcome by old age and death,
one who possesses nothing and grasps at nothing.
This is the island,
there is no other; I call it Nibbāna,
the total destruction of old age and death.
Having understood this, those who are mindful and fully extinguished in this very life do not fall under the power of Māra.
“They are not followers of Māra.
This is the tenth inquiry, the Question of Kappa the Young Man. 11.
The Question of Jatukaṇṇi the Young Man.
“Having heard of the Hero who has no desire for sensual pleasures,
(thus said the Venerable Jatukaṇṇi),
I have come to ask about him who has crossed over the flood and has no longing.”
O Sahajanetta, speak of the state of peace;
O Blessed One, tell me this according to reality.
For the Blessed One, having overcome sensual desires, dwells [in peace].
Like the sun with its radiance [overcomes] the earth,
O one of vast wisdom, explain the Dhamma to me, who am of limited wisdom, so that I may understand it.
The complete abandoning of birth and aging in this world.
“Withdraw your greed for sensual pleasures,” said the Blessed One, Jatukaṇṇī.
Having seen renunciation as security,
let there be nothing whatsoever in you that is either grasped or rejected.
Dry up what is before you;
let there be nothing for you behind; if you do not grasp at anything in between, you will not come again to renewed existence.
You shall wander at peace,
O Brahmin, having completely abandoned all greed for name-and-form.
"The taints do not exist within him,
by which one would fall under the power of death. Thus ends the eleventh inquiry,
the Question of the Young Brahmin Jatukaṇṇī.
12. The Inquiry of the Young Brahmin Bhadrāvudha “Leaving home, cutting off craving,
and unshakable,” (said the Venerable Bhadrāvudha).
Having heard of the Naga who has abandoned delight, crossed the flood, is liberated,
and has cast off the cycle of time— the wise one— I entreat him; they shall turn away from here.
People from various lands have gathered here,
O Hero, longing for your words;
please explain them well to them.
"For this Dhamma is known by you.
"Subdue all craving for grasping," [said the Blessed One to Bhadrāvudha].
Above, below, across, and in the middle—
whatever in the world people cling to,
by that very thing Māra follows the person.
Therefore, understanding this,
a mindful bhikkhu should not cling to anything in the entire world,
seeing beings as attached to grasping.
"This generation is stuck in the realm of death.
Thus ends the twelfth inquiry, the Question of the Young Man Bhadrāvudha.
13. The Question of the Young Man Udaya.
“I meditated upon him who was seated, free from passion,
having done what was to be done, and free from taints,” said the Venerable Udaya.
One who has gone beyond all phenomena,
I have come to you with a question:
please explain the liberation through final knowledge.
“The breaking up of ignorance.
“The abandoning of sensual desires,” [said the Blessed One]. “Arising,” [said the Blessed One].
The dispelling of both forms of dejection, the removal of sloth,
and the warding off of remorse.
Purified by equanimity and mindfulness,
preceded by reflection on the nature of phenomena—
I declare this to be the liberation through final knowledge.
“The breaking of ignorance.
“What is the fetter of the world?
What is its investigation?”
“By the abandoning of craving,
it is called Nibbāna.
“The world is bound by delight;”
The investigation of thought;
through the complete abandoning of craving,
it is called Nibbāna.”
“How does consciousness cease for one who dwells mindful?
Having approached to ask the Blessed One, [I inquire].”
“Let us hear those words of yours”:
“For one who does not delight in feeling, whether internal or external;”
“For one who lives thus,
consciousness ceases.
The Thirteenth Inquiry of the Young Man Udaya.
14. The Question of the Young Man Posāla “He who points out the past...
(Thus spoke the Venerable Posāla.)
Unshaken, with doubts severed,
having reached the further shore of all phenomena—
I have come to you with a question.
For one who has stilled the perception of form,
who has abandoned the entire body,
both internally and externally—
"To one who sees: 'There is nothing at all'—I ask about his knowledge:
how is such a person to be understood?"
“Having directly known all stations of consciousness,
O Posāla,” said the Blessed One,
“the Tathāgata [is liberated].”
One knows him as he stands,
liberated, with that as his final goal;
having known the arising of nothingness—
"Delight is a fetter"—
having directly known this thus,
one then sees it clearly with insight therein.
"This is the true knowledge of that brahmin who has lived the holy life.
The Fourteenth: The Question of the Young Man Posāla.
15. The Question of the Young Brahmin Mogharāja “I shall ask Sakka,” [said the venerable Mogharāja].
The One with Vision did not answer me;
O Queen, I have heard that he answered me only upon being asked a third time.
This world, the other world,
and the Brahma-world with its devas—
you do not understand their view.
Of the illustrious Gotama.
Thus, having come with a question regarding one whose vision is so excellent, I have approached you.
“How beholding the world does the King of Death not see him?
“Behold the world as empty;”
O Mogharāja, always mindful,
having uprooted the view of a self,
one may thus be a crosser over death.
“Thus beholding the world,
the King of Death does not see him.
The fifteenth inquiry of the young brahmin Mogharāja.
16. The Inquiry of the Young Brahmin Piṅgiya “I am old,
weak, and my complexion has faded,” (said the Venerable Piṅgiya).
My vision is not clear, my hearing is not at ease;
lest I perish, bewildered along the way,
teach me the Dhamma so that I may understand it.
“The abandoning here of birth and old age.
“Having seen beings being afflicted among forms,” said the Blessed One, “Piṅgiya.”
“Negligent people are crushed by forms;
therefore, Piṅgiya, being diligent,
abandon form so that there is no further becoming.”
“In the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions,
above and below— these ten directions:
there is nothing unseen, unheard, or unknown to you.”
Furthermore, there is nothing in the world that is not understood;
teach me the Dhamma so that I may know it—
the relinquishing of birth and old age right here.
“Beholding human beings overcome by craving,
(Piṅgiya, said the Blessed One,) born of anguish and enveloped by old age;”
Therefore, O Piṅgiya, being diligent,
abandon craving for the sake of no further becoming.
Thus ends the sixteenth inquiry, the Question of the Young Brahmin Piṅgiya.
